About Me

I believe great customer relationships are built long before a customer decides to stay.

Suzan Akpata

I've always been drawn to work that brings people, communication and problem-solving together. Over the past five years, I've built my experience across Customer Success, Account Management, sales, insurance and business operations, working with different teams and clients to make sure things don't just get started, but are followed through properly.

For me, customer success goes beyond answering questions or resolving complaints. It is about understanding what matters to each customer, paying attention to the details, recognising when something needs attention and taking action before a small issue becomes a bigger one. It means being someone clients can rely on, someone who communicates clearly, takes ownership and makes sure nothing important falls through the cracks.

Throughout my career, I've managed client accounts, coordinated service delivery, supported onboarding, maintained customer relationships, handled follow-ups and worked with CRM platforms to keep customer information and processes organised. At Aspen Field Services, for example, I coordinated nationwide inspection assignments and managed more than 50 client accounts weekly, keeping communication, scheduling and delivery moving together.

My journey has also taken me through financial services, real estate, insurance and technology. Each experience has taught me something valuable about people, business needs and the importance of consistency. I bring that perspective into every role, combining relationship-building with organisation, curiosity and a practical approach to solving problems.

I hold a B.Tech in Geology and am currently pursuing an MBA in Finance and Investment. My professional journey may not have followed a straight line, but it has given me a broader understanding of how people, processes and business decisions connect.

Proof, shown as it was built.

Workflows and portfolio views from HubSpot and Gainsight, plus one clearly labelled illustrative case. Click any screenshot to enlarge it.

HubSpot

A closed deal shouldn't land as a surprise.

The handoff from sales to success is where a good first impression is won or lost. So I built a HubSpot workflow that starts the moment a deal is won.

The challenge
Handoffs depended on people remembering every step, so onboarding started differently each time.
What I built
One workflow that creates the onboarding ticket, assigns ownership, sets up the customer plan, sends the welcome email and creates a task to prepare the kickoff.
The outcome
A consistent, structured move from sales to onboarding, with the same first steps for every customer.

The onboarding pipeline the workflow feeds.

Gainsight

Knowing who needs you before they ask.

With a portfolio of high-value customers, time is the scarce thing. I used account data to decide who needed me first.

The challenge
Knowing which accounts needed attention before they asked for it.
What I tracked
Health scores, ARR, lifecycle stage, renewal dates, engagement and last-touch activity.
The outcome
Proactive outreach where it mattered, earlier spotting of accounts needing attention, and a clearer view of renewals.
Gainsight

Customer goals, with an owner and a date.

A customer's objectives shouldn't live in anyone's memory. I put them in Success Plans where everyone could see them.

What I built
Success Plans around customer objectives: ROI, NPS, cost reduction and product adoption.
What I monitored
Progress, ownership, deadlines and overdue objectives.
The outcome
Customer outcomes stayed visible, and risks surfaced early instead of at renewal.
Illustrative engagement. Nova Health is not a real client or employer.

When "at risk" really meant "broken".

The situation
Eight clinics had gone quiet on a scheduling and reminder product after early adoption stalled.
The problem
Reminder workflows were not being used as intended, and nobody had looked into why.
What I found
A configuration issue in the reminder workflow was failing silently for a group of the clinics.
My strategy
Treat it as a product configuration recovery, not only a relationship problem.
The process
A 90 day recovery: correct the workflow, re-onboard clinic staff, monitor usage every week.
What I did
  • Found the root cause of the reminder failure
  • Retrained clinic staff on the corrected workflow
  • Checked usage weekly through the recovery window
  • Told each clinic exactly what broke and how it was fixed
The result
All eight clinics returned to active use once the workflow issue was fixed.
What I would do next
Add an automated check for this failure so it is caught before adoption stalls.

"At risk" can sometimes mean something is broken, not that the customer has lost interest.

How I think about customer success.

It isn't answering the question in front of me. It's knowing what the customer is trying to get done, and checking they're getting there.

Listen firstUnderstand what the customer actually needs.

Earn trustSay what I will do, then do it.

Start wellA smooth onboarding sets the tone for the account.

Watch engagementQuiet accounts are telling me something.

Spot risk earlyRaise it while there is still time to fix it.

Keep talkingRegular, plain communication, not only when there is news.

Coordinate fixesBring the right people together and follow through.

Show the valueMake sure customers keep seeing why they chose us.
